extracted.intended_audience: ERC grant applicants (researchers preparing ERC proposals)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for applicants on how to interpret ERC evaluation reports and the evaluation process (how many reviewers, how reviewers are chosen, when you can update information, and whether to exclude reviewers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of reviewers by evaluation step and score
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, ERC applications that get score “A” in step 2 are reviewed by 9-10 reviewers. Applications that were rejected with score “B” in the step 2 of the evaluation were reviewed by about 6-7 reviewers. Applications that were rejected with score “B” or “C” in step 1 of the evaluation process were reviewed by 3-4 reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading an evaluation report, consider how many reviewers were involved (it varies by step and score) — this affects how representative and diverse the assessments likely are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection process
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewers are being selected according to their CV. The panel members will look in the EC database or elsewhere to make sure they find the best reviewers to review your application. On top of that, the panel members will use the abstract of the ERC application, and the free keywords provided with the application to mutually evaluate with the selected reviewers whether they can evaluate your application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels use CVs, databases, the application abstract, and free keywords to choose reviewers; ensure your abstract and keywords accurately reflect your work so appropriate reviewers are chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise may be close but not identical
rubrics_metrics.description: They should be. The selection process aims to ensure that the best available reviewers will review your application. Many times this is indeed the case, but sometimes it is not. It happens that the selected reviewers are not the best one to carry out the work. Their CV, knowledge and expertise might be in the vicinity of your field, but not fully overlapping with yours. These reviewers may not have all the tools to fully evaluate your application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare your application with the possibility of partially-matched reviewers in mind: explain key concepts clearly and highlight the aspects you want reviewers to appreciate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluding reviewers (up to 3) and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fine to exclude a reviewer if you have a very good reason to do so (note that you don’t have to specify the reason for exclusion). However, keep in mind that such an excluded reviewer might be a panel member on the review panel that is supposed to evaluate your application. Officially, in case you decide to exclude a reviewer, this reviewer will not review your application. However, if this excluded reviewer is also a panel member, there is a chance that it will badly influence the other panel members, when referring to your application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can exclude up to 3 reviewers but do so only for very good reasons; weigh the risk that an excluded person who is a panel member could indirectly influence the panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: No official channel to add new information after submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Officially and technically the answer is No. After the deadline for submission, the system blocks any option to send any new information or updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although you cannot submit updates through the system after the deadline, you can indirectly convey new information by updating your personal website/webpage because many reviewers may google you; update your site as soon as possible with any relevant new findings or publications.
